title: Public housing stock: 1.5 million homes in 12 years
detail: Spend 1% of GDP a year (about €17 billion) on a public rental stock (*parque público de vivienda*): building, pre-emptive purchase rights (*tanteo y retracto*), empty homes, denser building and expropriation. 1.5 million public homes in 12 years (125,000 a year), with public rents of at most €600 a month.
c: €17 billion a year is, in our estimate, several times what the state now spends on housing, and does not fit the budget plan agreed with the EU without new taxes. 125,000 homes a year is more than the whole country now completes (100,980 in 2024).

s.t: Housing Ministry: Observatorio de Vivienda y Suelo, annual bulletin 2024 (La Moncloa)

title: Expropriate homes from large corporate landlords
detail: A law to expropriate homes from private corporations in phases: first owners of more than 1,000 homes, then more than 700, then companies with more than 50 properties. All urban buildings and residential land of *SAREB* (the "bad bank") would go to the state housing company Casa 47.
c: Expropriation is allowed only for public benefit and with full compensation (art. 33 of the Constitution); buying out large owners would, in our estimate, cost tens of billions of euros. Applying it by owner size would be challenged as arbitrary and as a breach of EU free movement of capital.

title: Phase out tourist flats within 3 years
detail: End all tourist-flat licences (*VUT*) and abusive "seasonal" lets (*alquiler de temporada*) in residential buildings in stressed areas within 3 years. Tourist lets would pay 21% VAT and up to 150% extra property tax (*IBI*); any let of 30 days or less would count as tourist use.
c: Tourist-flat licences are issued by regions and town halls. Catalonia sharply restricted them (Decreto-ley 3/2023) and the Constitutional Court upheld it (ruling 64/2025). But the state has no such power nationwide.

s.t: Constitutional Court ruling 64/2025: Catalan decree on tourist flats (BOE)

title: Rent cap: 25% of local household income
detail: In stressed areas the maximum rent would be the lower of 25% of average net household income in the census tract (*sección censal*) or the limit from the official SERPAVI index. The programme expects an average 35% drop in market rents, plus a further 30% cut in cities over 200,000 people or with heavy tourism.
c: A hard cap set by neighbourhood income rather than the market goes further than today's index. Berlin's rent cap was struck down by a court in 2021, and rents just outside the city rose sharply; findings on whether supply shrank in Catalonia differ.

s.t: Hahn, Kholodilin, Waltl, Fongoni, Management Science 70 (2024): the Berlin rent freeze
Monras, Montalvo (2023), Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco WP 2023-28: rent control in Catalonia
Jofre-Monseny, Martínez-Mazza, Segú (2023), Universitat de Barcelona: rent control in Catalonia

title: 10% annual tax on large landlords' homes
detail: A 10% charge on the value of homes: for companies from the first property, for individuals from the fourth if the total exceeds €800,000. Homes in stable affordable rental are exempt. Also scraps the special *SOCIMI* (property investment trust) regime.
c: 10% of the value every year is in effect a confiscatory tax, and the Constitution bars taxes with confiscatory effect (art. 31.1). The likely result is sell-offs and capital flight rather than affordable rentals.

title: 20% minimum corporate tax for large companies
detail: An effective minimum of 20% on adjusted accounting profit (instead of 15% today) for large groups, with no rise for small firms (*pymes*). Ends tax consolidation of groups and limits loss carry-forward to 4 years.
c: An EU directive sets a 15% minimum; going higher is allowed. Spain already introduced a 15% minimum tax in 2025. 20% would raise taxes on groups, but is realistic only with a majority.
pos: Large companies pay more, with less room for tax planning.
neg: Spain would sit above the OECD global minimum (15%): a risk of profits and investment moving elsewhere.

s.t: Directive (EU) 2022/2523 on the global minimum tax (BOE copy of the OJEU)
Ley 7/2024: 15% minimum tax and permanent bank levy (BOE)

title: Wealth tax from €1 million
detail: The large fortunes tax (*Impuesto de Solidaridad de las Grandes Fortunas*) would start at €1 million of net assets instead of €3 million (with a €700,000 allowance), with a minimum 2% on all fortunes above €1 million, and higher rates from €50 million. It would be a state tax that regional rebates cannot cancel.
c: The solidarity tax already exists (from €3 million). Lowering the threshold to €1 million would, in our estimate, reach hundreds of thousands of people, mostly through homes and businesses; regions with a wealth tax will offset it in their own way.
pos: More revenue from the wealthy and less inequality.
neg: In our estimate, a tax from €1 million would also reach middle-class owners of a pricey flat in Madrid or Barcelona, and gives wealth an incentive to leave.

s.t: Ley 38/2022: solidarity tax on large fortunes, bank and energy levies (BOE)

title: Lower income tax up to €27,000, up to 52% at the top; end the Beckham regime
detail: No income tax (*IRPF*) on the minimum wage, with relief tapering off at €27,000 (1.5 × SMI). New bands from €120,000 and a top state rate of 52% from €300,000. Capital income taxed closer to wages. Abolish the special regime for inbound workers (*régimen de trabajadores desplazados*, the "Beckham law") and deductions for private pension plans.
c: Technically simple, but 52% on the state portion alone, plus the regional portion, would in our estimate push top marginal rates above 60% in some regions: one of the highest in the EU.
pos: No income tax on the minimum wage; more money for low earners.
neg: A 52% rate would, in our estimate, be one of the highest in Europe: an incentive for high earners to leave or restructure.

title: Retirement age back to 65
detail: Return the retirement age (*edad de jubilación*) to 65 (the 2011 reform raised it); access from 60 for hard jobs such as construction, cleaning and fishing; no early-retirement penalties (*coeficientes reductores*) for people with more than 40 years of contributions.
c: Returning to 65 for everyone would, in our estimate, cost about 1–2% of GDP a year by 2040 and clash with the pension commitments in the EU recovery plan. The age is already 65 for people with 38.5 years of contributions.

s.t: Real Decreto Legislativo 8/2015, General Social Security Law (BOE)

title: 37.5-hour week now, 32 hours as the goal
detail: An immediate move to 37.5 hours, and 35 hours in the public sector, with no pay cut; overtime could not be paid in place of time off. Then a gradual cut to 32 hours a week.
c: 37.5 hours already failed in Congress in 2025; 32 hours has no chance. Moving public employees to 35 hours is up to the regions.

s.t: Congress, BOCG 15-A-58-3: 37.5-hour bill returned to the government (10 Sep 2025)

title: A permanent regularisation procedure
detail: Finish processing the 2026 extraordinary regularisation, reform the Immigration Law (*Ley de Extranjería*) and create a permanent, regulated route to legal status (*regularización*). Appointments at immigration offices within 7 calendar days through a free public booking system.
c: A permanent regularisation needs an organic law (176 votes). PP and Vox are against; impossible without PSOE and the nationalist parties. EU law does not ban regularisation, but several EU states criticise mass ones.
pos: Fewer people in the shadow economy: more tax and contributions, less exploitation.
neg: A permanent route may strengthen the "pull effect" (evidence on its size is disputed), and puts heavy pressure on offices, as in the 2026 regularisation (1.17 million applications).

s.t: La Moncloa, 2 Jul 2026: 1,174,978 regularisation applications filed

title: Remove barriers: *padrón*, bank account, diplomas
detail: Flexible town-hall registration (*empadronamiento*), a right to a free basic bank account (*cuenta de pago básica*), faster recognition of foreign qualifications (*homologación de títulos*), and an obligation for firms and offices to accept migrants' documents.
c: A basic account is already guaranteed by an EU directive; easier registration is mostly up to town halls.
pos: Migrants integrate faster and can work in jobs that match their qualifications.
neg: More work for town halls; easier registration without address checks makes fake registrations easier.

title: Three hours of free electricity a day
detail: Free power for all households during sunny hours with surplus supply. A public retailer (*comercializadora pública*) would offer 3 free hours a day and large retailers would have to include them; the competition authority CNMC would make sure other hours do not get dearer.
c: Free hours are an interesting idea (some tariffs already do this), but forcing every retailer to offer them conflicts with the EU electricity market directive (prices are set by the market).

title: Close Almaraz nuclear plant in 2027–28; phase out fossil fuels
detail: Close Almaraz I and II on schedule with no tax breaks; end fossil-fuel subsidies, retire gas plants (*ciclos combinados*) by 2045 and ban imports of fracked gas.
c: In August 2026 the government extended Almaraz to June 2030 (Orden TED/864/2026), so closing it in 2027–28 would mean revoking the permit. In our estimate the risk is higher prices and more reliance on gas; phasing out gas by 2045 is realistic.
pos: Less nuclear waste and fossil fuel; a faster energy transition.
neg: Revoking the 2030 permit would mean disputes with the owners. In our estimate the plant supplies about 5–7% of output; without replacement ready, prices and emissions may rise.

s.t: Orden TED/864/2026: Almaraz extended to 8 June 2030 (BOE)
REE, March 2026: the Spanish electricity system in 2025 (renewables 55.5%, nuclear 19%)
